snippets.text: Seal a hundred and forty-five people in a steel tube, and the air goes bad in two separate ways — and making oxygen only fixes one of them.
snippets.spoken: Seal a hundred and forty-five people in a steel tube, and the air goes bad in two separate ways — and making oxygen only fixes one of them.

snippets.text: The other is carbon dioxide — and the biggest source on board is the crew's own breath.
snippets.spoken: The other is carbon dioxide — and the biggest source on board is the crew's own breath.

snippets.text: So air is pushed through a scrubber containing an amine, which grabs carbon dioxide. Heat it, and the gas is released and pumped out of the boat.
snippets.spoken: So air is pushed through a scrubber containing an amine, which grabs carbon dioxide. Heat it, and the gas is released and pumped out of the boat.

snippets.text: Even then, it's never zero: in data reported in 2003, US nuclear submarines averaged several times the carbon dioxide of outdoor air.
snippets.spoken: Even then, it's never zero: in data reported in 2003, U.S. nuclear submarines averaged several times the carbon dioxide of outdoor air.

snippets.text: That's why a submarine needs two machines for its air: one to make oxygen, and one to pull carbon dioxide back out.
snippets.spoken: That's why a submarine needs two machines for its air: one to make oxygen, and one to pull carbon dioxide back out.

snippets.text: Once a submarine dives, GPS is gone.
snippets.spoken: Once a submarine dives, GPS is gone.

snippets.text: GPS works by radio, and seawater soaks up radio — its signals can't reach a submerged submarine.
snippets.spoken: GPS works by radio, and seawater soaks up radio — its signals can't reach a submerged submarine.

snippets.text: So the boat keeps track of itself. Gyroscopes sense every turn, accelerometers sense every push and pull, and a computer adds it all up.
snippets.spoken: So the boat keeps track of itself. Gyroscopes sense every turn, accelerometers sense every push and pull, and a computer adds it all up.

snippets.text: The catch: tiny errors add up too, and the estimate slowly drifts.
snippets.spoken: The catch: tiny errors add up too, and the estimate slowly drifts.

snippets.text: So every so often it checks against something outside — for example, coming up near the surface for a GPS fix, or matching the seafloor below to a map. Methods vary between navies and boats.
snippets.spoken: So every so often it checks against something outside — for example, coming up near the surface for a GPS fix, or matching the seafloor below to a map. Methods vary between navies and boats.

snippets.text: Sense the motion, add it up, then check it — that's how a submarine finds its way without GPS.
snippets.spoken: Sense the motion, add it up, then check it — that's how a submarine finds its way without GPS.

snippets.text: Seawater soaks up radio — so how does a hidden submarine get a message?
snippets.spoken: Seawater soaks up radio — so how does a hidden submarine get a message?

snippets.text: The higher the frequency, the faster it disappears. Very-low-frequency radio gets in — but, according to the US Navy, only tens of feet.
snippets.spoken: The higher the frequency, the faster it disappears. Very-low-frequency radio gets in — but, according to the U.S. Navy, only tens of feet.

snippets.text: So to listen, a submarine has to get an antenna up near the surface — which limits how deep and fast it can go, and makes it easier to spot.
snippets.spoken: So to listen, a submarine has to get an antenna up near the surface — which limits how deep and fast it can go, and makes it easier to spot.

snippets.text: The US also ran an extremely-low-frequency system, at about 76 hertz, that reached submarines hundreds of feet down — but only one way, slowly. It was shut down in 2004.
snippets.spoken: The U.S. also ran an extremely-low-frequency system, at about seventy-six hertz, that reached submarines hundreds of feet down — but only one way, slowly. It was shut down in 2004.

snippets.text: So every message to a hidden submarine is a trade: to hear it, the boat gives up some depth, speed or stealth.
snippets.spoken: So every message to a hidden submarine is a trade: to hear it, the boat gives up some depth, speed or stealth.

snippets.text: A nuclear submarine makes its own oxygen — by splitting water.
snippets.spoken: A nuclear submarine makes its own oxygen — by splitting water.

snippets.text: An electrolyser runs electric current through water and splits it into oxygen and hydrogen.
snippets.spoken: An electrolyser runs electric current through water and splits it into oxygen and hydrogen.

snippets.text: The oxygen goes into the air. The hydrogen is explosive in enough quantity, so on US submarines it's sent out of the boat, into the sea.
snippets.spoken: The oxygen goes into the air. The hydrogen is explosive in enough quantity, so on U.S. submarines it's sent out of the boat, into the sea.

snippets.text: And oxygen is held close to normal air: too little dulls thinking, too much makes fires more dangerous.
snippets.spoken: And oxygen is held close to normal air: too little dulls thinking, too much makes fires more dangerous.

snippets.text: Water and electricity — that's how a nuclear submarine makes the oxygen its crew breathes.
snippets.spoken: Water and electricity — that's how a nuclear submarine makes the oxygen its crew breathes.

snippets.text: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere of pressure.
snippets.spoken: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere of pressure.

snippets.text: So the part of a submarine that holds the sea back — the pressure hull — is a round steel tube, braced by rings of steel frames.
snippets.spoken: So the part of a submarine that holds the sea back — the pressure hull — is a round steel tube, braced by rings of steel frames.

snippets.text: Engineers design it so the shell can't buckle inward or crumple.
snippets.spoken: Engineers design it so the shell can't buckle inward or crumple.

snippets.text: How deep real submarines go isn't published — but at any depth, it's that ring-braced steel tube holding the sea back.
snippets.spoken: How deep real submarines go isn't published — but at any depth, it's that ring-braced steel tube holding the sea back.

snippets.text: A US Virginia-class submarine is three hundred and seventy-seven feet long — about the length of a football field. So how does something that big stay hidden underwater?
snippets.spoken: A U.S. Virginia-class submarine is three hundred and seventy-seven feet long — about the length of a football field. So how does something that big stay hidden underwater?

snippets.text: Water carries sound remarkably well. Low-frequency sound loses very little energy to absorption, so low rumbles can be detected a long way off; higher-pitched sounds fade much sooner.
snippets.spoken: Water carries sound remarkably well. Low-frequency sound loses very little energy to absorption, so low rumbles can be detected a long way off; higher-pitched sounds fade much sooner.

snippets.text: Many submarines are wrapped in special coatings. Some soak up incoming sonar pings, so less sound echoes back. Others muffle the noise the boat itself makes.
snippets.spoken: Many submarines are wrapped in special coatings. Some soak up incoming sonar pings, so less sound echoes back. Others muffle the noise the boat itself makes.

snippets.text: It doesn't make a submarine silent. It makes it harder to hear — and harder to find.
snippets.spoken: It doesn't make a submarine silent. It makes it harder to hear — and harder to find.

snippets.text: A nuclear submarine cleans its own air, and today's reactor cores are rated for over a million miles — so why does it ever come home?
snippets.spoken: A nuclear submarine cleans its own air, and today's reactor cores are rated for over a million miles — so why does it ever come home?

snippets.text: Unlike surface warships, submarines are almost never resupplied at sea. Everything the crew will eat is loaded before they leave.
snippets.spoken: Unlike surface warships, submarines are almost never resupplied at sea. Everything the crew will eat is loaded before they leave.

snippets.text: Crews and machines need time ashore too: US ballistic-missile submarines average 77 days at sea, then 35 in port for maintenance, with two crews taking turns.
snippets.spoken: Crews and machines need time ashore too: U.S. ballistic-missile submarines average seventy-seven days at sea, then thirty-five in port for maintenance, with two crews taking turns.

snippets.text: Food, maintenance, the people aboard and the mission — those set the clock.
snippets.spoken: Food, maintenance, the people aboard and the mission — those set the clock.
